overview.text: Mass spectrometry (MS) is a family of analytical methods used to study what a sample contains. In a typical experiment, molecules are turned into gas-phase ions, separated according to their mass-to-charge ratios, and detected. The resulting mass spectrum displays signals from the detected ions; scientists use its peaks to investigate the masses and composition of substances. Different instruments and ionization methods suit different samples, so MS is not one single machine or procedure. It is significant in fields including chemistry and materials science, and can help identify components in complex mixtures. When paired with gas chromatography, it can analyze mixtures by separating their components before mass analysis.

key_facts.text: A mass spectrometer’s core tasks are creating ions, separating them by mass-to-charge ratio, and detecting them.
A basic mass spectrum plots detected-ion counts against mass-to-charge ratio.
Ionization methods include MALDI, which uses laser energy, and electrospray, which uses a strong electric field.
In gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, the mixture is separated into components before ions are analyzed; the resulting patterns can help identify its chemical makeup.
Early mass-spectrometry research provided the first evidence for stable, nonradioactive isotopes.
